lead: A stepper motor turns in fixed angular steps. Each pulse from the driver advances the shaft by one step, and the controller counts pulses to know position without feedback. A servo motor closes a loop: an encoder or potentiometer reports the shaft angle, the drive compares it with the command, and the motor corrects the error. Steppers suit cheap positioning in printers, 3D printers and small CNC tables. Servos suit robot joints, conveyor tracking and machine tools where load changes and accuracy must hold. In hospitals, steppers drive syringe and infusion pumps, and servos move surgical robots, X-ray tables and CT gantries.
prereq: You need solenoids, relays and motors for motor torque, back emf and the idea of a rotating magnetic field.

sections.h3: Step angle, types and phase sequence

blocks.text: A stepper motor turns in discrete angular steps. Its rotor aligns with the magnetic field set by stator phases. Energise the phases in a fixed order and the rotor jumps from one stable position to the next. The step angle is the angle of one jump.

blocks.where: θ<sub>s</sub> is the step angle in degrees; N is the number of full steps per revolution.

blocks.text: Three common constructions exist. A variable-reluctance motor uses a soft-iron rotor and gives small steps but low torque. A permanent-magnet motor uses a magnet rotor and gives more torque. A hybrid motor combines both and is common at 1.8° per step, that is 200 steps per revolution.

Full-step drive energises one or two phases at a time. The figure shows a one-phase-on sequence: A, then B, then A′, then B′. A′ means A-bar, the opposite phase. Half-step drive alternates one-phase and two-phase states, so the shaft moves half a step each time. Microstepping drives two phases with sine and cosine currents. The field moves smoothly between full-step positions. The commanded increment becomes smaller, but the incremental torque for a small move is small too.

Pull-in torque is the largest load torque at which the motor can start and run without losing steps at a given pulse rate. Pull-out torque is the largest torque it can hold while running after it has started. Pull-in is lower than pull-out. Torque falls as the stepping rate rises because winding inductance limits current build-up. Near the natural frequency the rotor can resonate and lose steps. Half-stepping or mechanical damping reduces this.

sections.h3: Servo motor: error, feedback and modes

blocks.text: Servo motor means a motor used inside a closed loop. A command r(t) sets the wanted position, speed or torque. A sensor measures the actual value y(t). The drive forms the error e(t) = r(t) − y(t) and applies current to reduce it. When e is zero, the shaft holds the command.
Feedback is a potentiometer for a cheap angle measurement, or an encoder for digital position counts. A resolver gives sine and cosine signals as the shaft turns.

DC servo uses a permanent-magnet DC motor with an encoder and a PWM drive. AC servo uses a synchronous motor with an encoder or resolver; the drive controls stator currents by field orientation. Three command modes are common. Position mode holds an angle. Speed mode holds revolutions per minute. Torque mode holds motor current, hence torque.

sections.h3: Speed, position and a lead screw

blocks.text: A lead screw converts rotation into straight motion. The lead p is the distance the nut travels in one revolution, in mm/rev. The pitch is the spacing of neighbouring threads; for a single-start screw the two are equal, and for a two-start screw the lead is twice the pitch. For a stepper with N steps per revolution, one step moves the table by p/N. If pulses arrive at f pulses per second, the shaft speed is n = f/N rev/s, where N must be the steps per revolution of the drive mode in use: 200 in full step, 400 in half step and 3200 at 1/16 microstepping for a 1.8° motor. The table speed is v = n p = f p/N.

blocks.where: v is table speed in mm/s; f is pulse frequency in pulses per second; p is the lead in mm/rev; N is steps per revolution.
d<sub>step</sub> is linear movement per step in mm; p is the lead in mm/rev; N is steps per revolution.

blocks.text: Use the same idea for a servo. An encoder with C counts per revolution gives table movement per count p/C. A command of M counts moves the table M p/C mm. This is why a servo can stop at a position even if the load changes: the encoder count is measured, not assumed. With microstepping, use commanded microsteps per revolution for resolution, but remember the mechanical step is still 360°/N.

figure.caption: Left: in full-step drive one stator phase is on at a time, and the rotor lines up with it. Right: the 1.8° motor turns a 5 mm lead screw, so 1000 pulses/s give 5 rev/s (300 rpm) and 25 mm/s, and each pulse moves the table 0.025 mm. Phases are drawn simplified; a real 1.8° motor has many rotor teeth.

spec.aria: A four-pole stator with phases A, B, C and D and a magnet rotor pointing to the energised phase A; a motor turning a lead screw with a nut and table moving at 25 millimetres per second; below, a staircase of table position rising 0.025 millimetres per pulse to 0.2 millimetres after 8 pulses.

examples.question: A stepper motor has a step angle of 1.8°. It is driven by 1000 pulses per second. The shaft turns a lead screw of pitch 5 mm. Find (a) steps per revolution, (b) shaft speed in rev/s and rpm, (c) table speed in mm/s, and (d) linear distance per step.
steps: Steps per revolution: N = 360° / θ<sub>s</sub> = 360° / 1.8° = 200 steps per revolution.
One pulse gives one step, so the step rate is 1000 steps per second.
Shaft speed: n = f / N = 1000 / 200 = 5 rev/s.
Table speed: v = n p = 5 rev/s × 5 mm/rev = 25 mm/s.
Linear distance per step: d<sub>step</sub> = p / N = 5 mm / 200 = 0.025 mm per step.
examples.answer: The motor has 200 steps per revolution, runs at 5 rev/s or 300 rpm, moves the table at 25 mm/s, and advances 0.025 mm per step.
examples.check:
step_angle = 1.8
pulse_rate = 1000
pitch = 5
spr = 360 / step_angle
n = pulse_rate / spr
rpm = n * 60
v = n * pitch
d_step = pitch / spr
print(int(spr))
print(int(n))
print(int(rpm))
print(int(v))
print(d_step)

examples.question: A syringe pump moves the plunger of a 50 mL syringe (inner diameter 26.7 mm) with a 1.8° stepper at 1/16 microstepping on a lead screw of 1 mm lead. Find (a) microsteps per revolution and plunger travel per microstep, (b) volume per microstep, and (c) the pulse rate for an infusion of 10 mL/h.
steps: (a) Full steps: 360 / 1.8 = 200 per revolution; microsteps: 200 × 16 = 3200 per revolution. Travel per microstep = 1 mm / 3200 = 3.125 × 10⁻⁴ mm = 0.3125 µm.
(b) Plunger area: A = π (26.7/2)² = π × 13.35² = 559.9 mm². Volume per microstep = 559.9 × 3.125 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.175 mm³ = 0.175 µL.
Pulse rate = speed × microsteps per mm = 4.961 × 10⁻³ × 3200 = 15.9 pulses per second.
Check: 15.9 pulses/s × 0.175 µL × 3600 s = 10 000 µL = 10 mL in one hour, as set.
examples.answer: 3200 microsteps per revolution, 0.3125 µm and 0.175 µL per microstep; 10 mL/h needs about 15.9 pulses per second.
examples.check:
import math
A = math.pi * (26.7 / 2)**2
print(200 * 16, 1000 / 3200)
print(round(A / 3200, 3))
print(round(10000 / A / 3600 * 3200, 1))

traps: Step angle is not the final resolution after microstepping. A 1.8° motor with 1/16 microstepping gives 0.1125° per commanded microstep, but the mechanical step is still 1.8° and small moves have low incremental torque.
Pull-in torque and pull-out torque are not the same. Pull-in is the limit for starting and running; pull-out is the limit while already running. Pull-in is lower.
Pulse frequency does not multiply speed by steps per revolution. Shaft speed is f/N rev/s, so more steps per revolution means slower speed for the same pulse rate.
Pitch and lead are equal only for a single-start screw; use the lead (travel per revolution), and use the steps per revolution of the drive mode actually set.
A servo drive with the feedback sign reversed drives the error larger, not smaller. The shaft runs away instead of holding position.

quiz.q: Define step angle of a stepper motor.
quiz.a: Step angle is the angular movement of the shaft for one full step, equal to 360° divided by the number of steps per revolution.

quiz.q: Why can a stepper motor lose position without any fault in the driver?
quiz.a: It is open loop. The controller counts pulses but does not measure the shaft. If the load exceeds pull-in or pull-out torque, or the pulse rate is too high, the rotor can slip and the count no longer matches the true position.

quiz.q: A stepper has a step angle of 0.9° and is driven at 800 pulses per second. Its lead screw pitch is 4 mm. Find the shaft speed in rpm and the table speed in mm/s.
A stepper starts a load at low speed but stalls when the pulse rate is ramped up quickly. Explain using pull-in and pull-out torque.
quiz.a: At a low pulse rate the pull-in torque is higher than the load torque, so it starts. At higher stepping rate the winding current cannot build up fully, so torque falls. A fast ramp demands more torque before the rotor reaches speed, and the load torque can exceed the pull-in torque at the rates it passes through. The motor then loses steps or stalls.

quiz.q: Name two feedback sensors used in servo motors.
quiz.a: A potentiometer and an encoder. A resolver is also used.

quiz.q: What is the difference between position mode and torque mode in a servo drive?
quiz.a: Position mode holds a commanded shaft angle by closing the position loop. Torque mode holds a commanded motor current, which gives a commanded torque, and lets speed or position follow the load.

quiz.q: A servo encoder gives 2500 counts per revolution. The lead screw pitch is 10 mm. How many counts are needed to move the table 50 mm?
quiz.a: One revolution moves 10 mm, so 50 mm needs 5 revolutions. Counts = 5 × 2500 = 12500 counts.

quiz.q: Why does a stepper motor sometimes vibrate and lose steps near a particular pulse rate, and what simple change helps?
quiz.a: The pulse rate is near the rotor's natural frequency, so the rotor oscillates with large amplitude and can slip. Half-stepping, microstepping or added mechanical damping changes the excitation and reduces resonance.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial motion uses field-oriented control, closed-loop steppers with encoders, and integrated servo drives. Research looks at magnetic lead screws and ultrasonic motors for quiet, precise motion. Search terms: hybrid stepper, microstepping, resolver, field-oriented control, motion profile.
